chapters.title: Chapter 3: Calculating and Paying Advance Tax

lessons.title: Handling Unpredictable Income: Capital Gains, Windfalls and Mid-Year Changes

body.text: Real life does not follow the advance tax calendar. A flat gets sold in November, a quiz show pays out in January, a job ends in July. The law gives specific relief for income you could not have foreseen, and ordinary good sense handles the rest: when your income changes, change your estimate at the very next due date.

children.text: The first two lessons of this chapter assumed you could see your year coming. This one deals with the surprises. It shows which kinds of income the law treats as unpredictable, how to handle a large one-off gain, why windfalls with TDS rarely cause trouble, and what to do when your regular income rises or falls in the middle of the year.
Income the Law Treats as Unpredictable

markDefs.definition: Winnings from lotteries, crossword puzzles, game shows, card games, races and similar sources. Taxed at a flat 30% plus cess, with no basic exemption and no deductions.

children.text: Section 425 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (old section 234C) carries a relief for three kinds of income. If an instalment falls short because of capital gains, dividends or
that arose after that instalment's due date, no interest is charged for the earlier instalment, provided the tax on that income is paid in the remaining instalments, or by 31 March if none remain.

body.caption: Which income gets the timing relief

cells: Capital gains on shares, mutual funds, property or gold
Yes
The gain only exists once you decide to sell
Dividends
Yes
Amount and timing are decided by the company, not you
Lottery, game show and other casual winnings
Yes
Impossible to predict
Salary, bonus, pension
No
Regular income, and usually covered by TDS anyway
Rent and FD interest
No
Predictable from agreements and deposit rates
Freelance, business, F&O and intraday income
No
Business income is expected to be estimated through the year

body.text: The relief is about timing, not rate. It never reduces the tax itself. It only stops the law from charging you interest for failing to pay tax on income that did not exist yet. Miss the next instalment after the income arises, and the relief is gone.

body.title: Quick Check: Relief or No Relief?
body.question: Four taxpayers each paid nothing on 15 June and had a large increase in income in July. Who is protected from interest on the June instalment, provided they pay the tax on that income by 15 September?
options: Lata, whose tenant signed a new lease in July at double the rent
Imran, who received a large special dividend from a listed company in July
Neeraj, whose F&O trading turned sharply profitable in July
Sonal, whose FD matured in July and was reinvested at a higher rate
body.explanation: Dividends are one of the three income types covered by the relief, along with capital gains and casual income. Rent, business income such as F&O, and interest are not covered. For those, the June instalment should reflect a reasonable estimate of the full year, and any shortfall attracts interest.

children.text: Sunil, a salaried operations head in Pune earning ₹15,00,000, has his salary TDS fully in order and had no advance tax liability. On 20 November 2026 he sells a flat he bought in 2016 for ₹90,00,000, for ₹1,20,00,000. The buyer deducts 1% TDS because the price is ₹50 lakh or more.

children.text: Because the flat was bought before 23 July 2024, Sunil, as a resident individual, may instead choose 20% with indexation if that gives lower tax. His total income stays below ₹50 lakh, so no surcharge applies. If he plans to reinvest the gain in another house or in specified bonds within the permitted time, an exemption may reduce the tax, but he should only count that in his estimate once the reinvestment is genuinely committed.

body.label: Tax on Sunil's sale not covered by TDS
body.context: The buyer's 1% TDS is calculated on the sale price, not the gain, so it covers less than a third of the tax here.

body.title: Try It: What TDS Leaves Behind
body.prompt: Revathi, in Chennai, sells a plot for ₹80 lakh that she bought for ₹50 lakh in 2015. Ignoring costs and indexation, her long-term gain is taxed at 12.5% plus 4% cess, and the buyer deducts 1% TDS on the sale price. How much tax on the gain is left uncovered by TDS? Answer in rupees.
body.explanation: The gain is ₹30,00,000. Tax at 12.5% is ₹3,75,000, and with 4% cess ₹3,90,000. TDS at 1% of ₹80,00,000 is ₹80,000. That leaves ₹3,10,000. The lower the sale price relative to the gain, the less TDS covers.

body.title: Sunil's advance tax after the sale

events.title: Nothing due
events.description: The sale had not happened. With salary TDS covering everything, he owed no advance tax on these dates.

events.title: Flat sold
events.description: The capital gain arises. Buyer deducts ₹1,20,000 TDS.

events.title: Pay tax on the gain
events.description: The safest course under the relief is to pay the full ₹2,70,000 with the December instalment, the next one after the gain arose.

events.title: Final check
events.description: Confirms the challan shows in AIS and adjusts if transfer costs or an exemption change the figure.

events.title: Report the sale
events.description: Declares the gain, claims the ₹1,20,000 TDS and the advance tax, with no interest for June or September.

children.text: Compare that with someone who knew from April that they would sell. They would have needed ₹40,500 by June, ₹1,21,500 by September and ₹2,02,500 by December. The relief is what allows Sunil to start at December without penalty.

Pooja, a school teacher in Nagpur, wins ₹25,00,000 on a television quiz show. Winnings like these are taxed at a flat 30% plus 4% cess, which is ₹7,80,000 on her prize, with no basic exemption and no deductions. The broadcaster must deduct TDS at 30% before paying her.

stats.label: Tax rate on casual winnings
stats.context: Flat, regardless of your slab, with no basic exemption

stats.label: TDS on winnings
stats.context: Deducted by the payer when a single winning exceeds ₹10,000

stats.label: Pooja's tax on ₹25,00,000
stats.context: Most of it already deducted at source before the prize reaches her

children.text: Because TDS on winnings is close to the final rate, most prize winners owe little or nothing more. Any small balance, for example cess or surcharge not covered by the deduction, is still covered by the casual income relief if paid by the next due date. Prizes given in kind, such as a car, are different: the payer must still ensure tax is deducted before handing over the prize, and the winner often has to fund that tax in cash.

body.title: Fill in the Blank: The Three Protected Incomes
body.textWithBlank: The timing relief for advance tax covers capital gains, dividends and ___ income such as lottery and game show winnings.
body.explanation: Casual income is the term for winnings from lotteries, puzzles, game shows, races and similar sources. Along with capital gains and dividends, it is treated as income you cannot reasonably predict at earlier instalment dates.

children.text: When Your Regular Income Changes Mid-Year

Salary, rent and business income do not get the timing relief, but they do get the flexibility of revision. At each due date, you are expected to base the cumulative payment on your best estimate at that moment. When income changes, revise at the very next date.

body.caption: Common mid-year changes and what to do
headers: What to do at the next due date

cells: You switch to a higher-paying job
Usually none if you declare your previous salary to the new employer
Give payroll your earlier salary and TDS details as soon as you join
You leave a job to go freelance
Freelance income has no TDS, so advance tax usually starts
Estimate the rest of the year's receipts and check whether the presumptive scheme applies
You take a sabbatical or lose your job
Estimated income falls, so the next cumulative amount may already be covered
Revise down and pay only if the new cumulative figure exceeds what you have paid
A tenant moves out and the flat sits empty
Rent estimate falls
Revise down; do not keep paying on the old rent
A large bonus is announced in January
Usually covered by TDS on salary
Check your payslip; only act if TDS does not cover it
A friend, not a relative, gifts you ₹2 lakh
Gifts from non-relatives above ₹50,000 in a year are taxable, and not covered by the timing relief
Add it to your estimate for the next due date

body.title: Income rises vs income falls in the middle of the year

columns.label: Income rises
points: Raise the estimate at the next due date and top up to the cumulative percentage
Earlier instalments may attract interest unless the rise is capital gains, dividends or casual income
The longer you wait to revise, the more instalments carry interest
Paying tax on the new income immediately is the cheapest fix

columns.label: Income falls
points: Revise the estimate down at the next due date
If you have already paid more than the new cumulative amount, pay nothing further for now
Advance tax already paid cannot be withdrawn during the year
Any excess comes back as a refund, with interest, after you file

children.text: Kiran, a Hyderabad-based consultant who keeps regular books, estimated advance tax of ₹1,80,000 in June and paid ₹27,000. In August she takes an unplanned six-month break, and her September estimate drops to ₹60,000. The 45% due by September is ₹27,000, which she has already paid, so she pays nothing in September. By December she needs 75%, or ₹45,000, so she pays ₹18,000 then.

body.title: Scenario: Arvind Goes Independent
body.scenario: Arvind is a software engineer in Bengaluru on a ₹24 lakh salary. He resigns at the end of July 2026, having been paid ₹8,00,000 in salary, on which his employer deducted ₹97,500 of TDS. From September he consults for two US companies, receiving ₹30,00,000 by March 2027, all by bank transfer with no TDS. As an IT professional he can use the presumptive scheme at 50%. He is on the new regime and had paid no advance tax, because in June his salary TDS covered everything.
body.prompt: How much advance tax does Arvind owe for tax year 2026-27, and by when? Is he at risk of interest for June and September?
body.modelAnswer: His total income is salary of ₹8,00,000 less the ₹75,000 standard deduction (₹7,25,000), plus presumptive professional income of 50% of ₹30,00,000 (₹15,00,000), giving ₹22,25,000. Slab tax is ₹2,56,250 (₹20,000 plus ₹40,000 plus ₹60,000 plus ₹80,000, and 25% of ₹2,25,000), or ₹2,66,500 with 4% cess. After ₹97,500 of salary TDS, ₹1,69,000 remains. Because he declares income under the presumptive scheme for the year, he can pay the whole of his advance tax by 15 March 2027, and interest for the June, September and December instalments does not arise. Consulting income is not covered by the timing relief, so without the presumptive scheme he would need to revise his estimate in September and catch up. The single March deadline is convenient, not a savings plan: with ₹1,69,000 due, he should set aside roughly 6% of every client payment from September onwards.

body.title: Within a Week of Any Unexpected Income
steps: Identify the type: capital gain, dividend or casual income gets the timing relief; salary, rent, interest, gifts and business income do not
Calculate the tax on it at the correct rate, including cess and any surcharge
Subtract any TDS deducted on it, such as 1% on a property sale or 30% on winnings
Add the balance to your estimate and pay it no later than the next advance tax due date, or by 31 March if none remain
If your regular income has fallen instead, revise down and skip payments until the new cumulative amount exceeds what you have paid
Save the sale deed, contract note, dividend advice or prize letter with the challan receipt

body.description: The department's guide to capital gains, including long-term gains on property, the choice of rates for property bought before 23 July 2024, and exemptions for reinvestment.

cards.definition: No interest for earlier instalments on capital gains, dividends or casual income arising later, if their tax is paid in the remaining instalments or by 31 March.
Winnings from lotteries, puzzles, game shows, card games and races, taxed at 30% plus cess with no basic exemption.
1% of the sale price, deducted by the buyer when the property is worth ₹50 lakh or more. Usually far less than the tax on the gain.
12.5% without indexation; residents selling property acquired before 23 July 2024 may choose 20% with indexation if lower.
When income falls, you pay only if the new cumulative amount exceeds what you have paid. Excess advance tax is refunded after filing.
Gifts from non-relatives above ₹50,000 in a year are taxable income and are not covered by the timing relief.

points: Capital gains, dividends and casual income get relief from interest on earlier instalments if their tax is paid at the next due date
The relief does not cover salary, rent, interest, gifts, or business income such as freelancing and F&O
TDS on a property sale is 1% of the price, so a large gain can leave most of the tax uncovered
Winnings carry TDS close to the final 30% rate, so they rarely leave a large balance
When regular income rises, revise at the next due date; when it falls, revise down and stop paying until the new cumulative figure catches up
Switching to presumptive consulting mid-year can move the whole advance tax deadline to 15 March, but set aside tax from every receipt

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and does not constitute tax, legal or investment advice. Section references are to the Income-tax Act, 2025, with the corresponding Income-tax Act, 1961 section in brackets. Examples ignore transfer costs, improvements, indexation and exemptions unless stated, and use rates for tax year 2026-27 as understood at the time of writing. Capital gains on property can be complex. Verify current rules or consult a qualified chartered accountant before acting.
